tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Do not set `run_in_background=true`; background task management tools are not available.

**Commands available:**
The following common command categories are usually available. Availability still depends on the host, so when in doubt run `which <command>` first to confirm a command exists before relying on it.
- Navigation and inspection: `ls`, `pwd`, `cd`, `stat`, `file`, `du`, `df`, `tree`
- File and directory management: `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `ln`, `chmod`, `chown`
- Text and data processing: `wc`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `diff`, `xargs`
- Archives and compression: `tar`, `gzip`, `gunzip`, `zip`, `unzip`
- Networking and transfer: `curl`, `wget`, `ping`, `ssh`, `scp`
- Version control: `git`; for GitHub-hosted work (PRs, issues, CI runs, API queries) prefer the `gh` CLI when installed — it carries the user's GitHub auth and can return structured JSON
- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

tools.description:
Search file contents using regular expressions (powered by ripgrep).

Use Grep when the task is to find unknown content or unknown file locations. Do not use shell `grep` or `rg` directly; this tool applies workspace path policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
ALWAYS use Grep tool instead of running `grep` or `rg` from a shell — direct shell calls bypass workspace policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
If you already know a concrete file path and need to inspect its contents, use Read directly instead.

Write patterns in ripgrep regex syntax, which differs from POSIX `grep` syntax. For example, braces are special, so escape them as `\{` to match a literal `{`.

Hidden files (dotfiles such as `.gitlab-ci.yml` or `.eslintrc.json`) are searched by default. To also search files excluded by `.gitignore` (such as `node_modules` or build outputs), set `include_ignored` to `true`. Read a text file from the local filesystem.

If the user provides a concrete file path to a text file, call Read directly. Do not `Glob`, `ls`, or otherwise pre-check known text file paths; missing or invalid file paths return errors you can handle. Do not use Read for directories; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob when you need files matching a name pattern (Glob lists files only, never directories). Use `Grep` only when the task is to search for unknown content or locations.

When you need several files, prefer to read them in parallel: emit multiple `Read` calls in a single response instead of reading one file per turn.

- Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute.
- Returns up to 1000 lines or 100 KB per call, whichever comes first; lines longer than 2000 chars are truncated mid-line.
- Page larger files with `line_offset` (1-based start line) and `n_lines`. Omit `n_lines` to read up to the 1000-line cap.

- Only UTF-8 text files can be read. Non-UTF-8 encodings, binary files, and files containing NUL bytes are refused; use `ReadMediaFile` for images or video, and Bash or an MCP tool for other binary formats.
- Negative line_offset reads from the end of the file (for example, -100 reads the last 100 lines); the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.
- Output format: `<line-number>\t<content>` per line.
- A `<system>...</system>` status block is appended after the file content; it summarizes how much was read (line and byte counts, truncation, line-ending notes) and is not part of the file itself.
- Pure CRLF files are displayed with LF line endings; `Edit` matches this output and preserves CRLF when writing back.
- Mixed or lone carriage-return line endings are shown as `\r` and require exact `Edit.old_string` escapes.
- After a successful `Edit`/`Write`, do not re-read solely to prove the write landed. When the task depends on an exact file, API, or output shape, inspect the final external contract before finishing.

path.description: Path to a text file. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute. Directories are not supported; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob for pattern search.

line_offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Omit to start at line 1. Negative values read from the end of the file; the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.

n_lines.description: The number of lines to read; the tool also applies its internal cap. Omit to read up to the internal cap of 1000 lines.

1	# richgo
2	
3	Rich-Go will enrich `go test` outputs with text decorations.
4	
5	[![asciicast](https://asciinema.org/a/99810.png)](https://asciinema.org/a/99810)
6	
7	## Description
8	
9	richgo is a command-line tool that adds color and formatting to the output of Go's `go test` command, making test results easier to read and understand.
10	
11	## Installation
12	
13	### Using go get
14	
15	```
16	go get -u github.com/kyoh86/richgo
17	```
18	
19	### Using homebrew
20	
21	```
22	brew install kyoh86/tap/richgo
23	```
24	
25	### Using asdf
26	
27	```
28	asdf plugin add richgo
29	asdf install richgo 0.3.6
30	```
31	
32	## Usage
33	
34	### Basic Usage
35	
36	```sh
37	richgo test ./...
38	```
39	
40	### In an existing pipeline
41	
42	If your build scripts expect to interact with the standard output format of `go test` (for instance, if you're using [go-junit-report](https://github.com/jstemmer/go-junit-report)), you'll need to use the `testfilter` subcommand of `richgo`.
43	
44	For example:
45	
46	```sh
47	go test ./... | tee >(richgo testfilter) | go-junit-report
48	```
49	
50	This will "tee" the output of the standard `go test` run into a `richgo testfilter` process as well as passing the original output to `go-junit-report`.
51	
52	### Creating an alias
53	
54	You can define an alias so that `go test` prints rich outputs:
55	
56	* bash: `~/.bashrc`
57	* zsh: `~/.zshrc`
58	
59	```
60	alias go=richgo
61	```
62	
63	## Configuration
64	
65	### Configuration file paths
66	
67	It's possible to change styles with a preference file. Rich-Go loads preferences from the files in the following order:
68	
69	* `${CWD}/.richstyle`
70	* `${CWD}/.richstyle.yaml`
71	* `${CWD}/.richstyle.yml`
72	* `${GOPATH}/.richstyle`
73	* `${GOPATH}/.richstyle.yaml`
74	* `${GOPATH}/.richstyle.yml`
75	* `${GOROOT}/.richstyle`
76	* `${GOROOT}/.richstyle.yaml`
77	* `${GOROOT}/.richstyle.yml`
78	* `${HOME}/.richstyle`
79	* `${HOME}/.richstyle.yaml`
80	* `${HOME}/.richstyle.yml`
81	
82	Setting the environment variable `RICHGO_LOCAL` to 1, Rich-Go loads only `${CWD}/.richstyle*`.
83	
84	### Configuration file format
85	
86	Rich-Go supports YAML formatted configuration files.
87	
88	```yaml
89	# Type of the label that notes a kind of each lines.
90	labelType: (long | short | none)
91	
92	# Style of "Build" lines.
93	buildStyle:
94	  # Hide lines
95	  hide: (true | false)
96	  # Bold or increased intensity.
97	  bold: (true | false)
98	  faint: (true | false)
99	  italic: (true | false)
100	  underline: (true | false)
101	  blinkSlow: (true | false)
102	  blinkRapid: (true | false)
103	  # Swap the foreground color and background color.
104	  inverse: (true | false)
105	  conceal: (true | false)
106	  crossOut: (true | false)
107	  frame: (true | false)
108	  encircle: (true | false)
109	  overline: (true | false)
110	  # Fore-color of text
111	  foreground: ("#xxxxxx" | rgb(0-256,0-256,0-256) | rgb(0x00-0xFF,0x00-0xFF,0x00-0xFF) | (name of colors))
112	  # Back-color of text
113	  background: # Same format as `foreground`
114	
115	# Style of the "Start" lines.
116	startStyle:
117	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
118	
119	# Style of the "Pass" lines.
120	passStyle:
121	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
122	
123	# Style of the "Fail" lines.
124	failStyle:
125	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
126	
127	# Style of the "Skip" lines.
128	skipStyle:
129	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
130	
131	# Style of the "File" lines.
132	fileStyle:
133	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
134	
135	# Style of the "Line" lines.
136	lineStyle:
137	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
138	
139	# Style of the "Pass" package lines.
140	passPackageStyle:
141	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
142	
143	# Style of the "Fail" package lines.
144	failPackageStyle:
145	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
146	
147	# A threshold of the coverage
148	coverThreshold: (0-100)
149	
150	# Style of the "Cover" lines with the coverage that is higher than coverThreshold.
151	coveredStyle:
152	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
153	
154	# Style of the "Cover" lines with the coverage that is lower than coverThreshold.
155	uncoveredStyle:
156	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
157	
158	# If you want to delete lines, write the regular expressions.
159	removals:
160	  - (regexp)
161	# If you want to leave `Test` prefixes, set it "true".
162	leaveTestPrefix: (true | false)
163	```
164	
165	### Line categories
166	
167	Rich-Go separates the output lines into the following categories:
168	
169	* **Build**: Build error messages
170	* **Start**: Test start lines (e.g., `=== RUN   TestSampleOK/SubtestOK`)
171	* **Pass**: Test pass lines (e.g., `--- PASS: TestSampleOK/SubtestOK`)
172	* **Fail**: Test failure lines (e.g., `--- FAIL: TestSampleNG (0.00s)`)
173	* **Skip**: Test skip lines (e.g., `--- SKIP: TestSampleSkip (0.00s)`)
174	* **PassPackage**: Package pass indicator (`PASS`)
175	* **FailPackage**: Package fail indicator (`FAIL`)
176	* **Cover**: Coverage analysis lines
177	
178	Each category can be styled separately.
179	
180	### Label types
181	
182	* **Long**: BUILD, START, PASS, FAIL, SKIP, COVER
183	* **Short**: !!, >, o, x, -, %
184	* **None**: Rich-Go will never output labels.
185	
186	### Default configuration
187	
188	```yaml
189	labelType: long
190	buildStyle:
191	  bold: true
192	  foreground: yellow
193	startStyle:
194	  foreground: lightBlack
195	passStyle:
196	  foreground: green
197	failStyle:
198	  bold: true
199	  foreground: red
200	skipStyle:
201	  foreground: lightBlack
202	passPackageStyle:
203	  foreground: green
204	  hide: true
205	failPackageStyle:
206	  bold: true
207	  foreground: red
208	  hide: true
209	coverThreshold: 50
210	coveredStyle:
211	  foreground: green
212	uncoveredStyle:
213	  bold: true
214	  foreground: yellow
215	fileStyle:
216	  foreground: cyan
217	lineStyle:
218	  foreground: magenta
219	```
220	
221	### Solarized Dark theme compatibility
222	
223	The bright-black is used for background color in Solarized dark theme. Richgo uses that color for "startStyle" and "skipStyle", so "START" and "SKIP" lines may not be visible on screens with Solarized dark theme.
224	
225	To resolve that conflict, you can set another color for "startStyle" and "skipStyle" in your `.richstyle` file:
226	
227	```yaml
228	startStyle:
229	  foreground: yellow
230	
231	skipStyle:
232	  foreground: lightYellow
233	```
234	
235	## Overriding colorization detection
236	
237	By default, `richgo` determines whether or not to colorize its output based on whether it's connected to a TTY or not. This works for most use cases, but may not behave as expected if you use `richgo` in a pipeline of commands.
238	
239	To force colorization, add `RICHGO_FORCE_COLOR=1` to the environment:
240	
241	```sh
242	RICHGO_FORCE_COLOR=1 richgo test ./... | tee test.log
243	```
244	
245	## Getting the version
246	
247	If you want to get the version of `richgo`, this information is embedded in the binary (since Go 1.18). You can view it with `go version -m`:
248	
249	```console
250	$ go version -m $(command -v richgo)
251	./richgo: go1.18
252		path	github.com/kyoh86/richgo
253		mod	github.com/kyoh86/richgo	v0.3.10	h1:iSGvcjhtQN2IVrBDhPk0if0R/RMQnCN1E/9OyAW4UUs=
254		[...]
255	```
256	
257	With POSIX `awk`:
258	
259	```console
260	$ go version -m $(command -v richgo) | awk '$1 == "mod" && $2 == "github.com/kyoh86/richgo" {print $3;}'
261	v0.3.10
262	```

Test harness: temp dir with `RICHGO_LOCAL=1` to isolate config; `RICHGO_FORCE_COLOR=1` for styled mode. Escapes shown as `ESC[...m`. All exit codes captured via pipe status, not the downstream pager.

## 1. `leaveTestPrefix`

**Only affects styled (colorized) output.** In plain mode (no TTY, no FORCE_COLOR) output is always byte-verbatim pass-through regardless of this setting.

- Default (`false` or absent): the literal prefix `Test` is stripped from the **first component only** of the test name on classified test lines (RUN/PASS/FAIL/SKIP). With `true`, the name is kept whole.
- The classification itself requires the name to begin with literal `Test` (case-sensitive) — with or without `leaveTestPrefix`:
  - `=== RUN   Testfoo` → `ESC[90mSTART| fooESC[0m`; `Testify` → `ify`; `Test` → `START| ` (empty name); `TestTest` → `Test` (only the first `Test` stripped).
  - `=== RUN   TEST`, `BenchmarkX`, `ExampleFoo`, `FuzzFoo` are **not classified at all** — they fall through to the "unknown line" rendering: `ESC[90m     | === RUN   TESTESC[0m` (5-space empty label + `| ` + raw line verbatim).
- Subtests: `TestFoo/SubBar` → `Foo/SubBar` (default) / `TestFoo/SubBar` (true). `TestFoo/TestSub` → `Foo/TestSub` — a `Test` prefix on later path components is never stripped. Output indent is depth-based, not from source whitespace: depth-1 → `START|   Foo/SubBar` (3 spaces), depth-2 → `START|     Foo/a_b/c` (5 spaces; i.e. 1+2·depth). This applied identically to `    --- PASS: TestFoo/SubBar (0.00s)` → `PASS |   Foo/SubBar (0.00s)`.
- Applies to RUN, PASS, FAIL, SKIP lines equally (`--- FAIL: TestFoo/SubFail (0.02s)` → `FAIL |   Foo/SubFail (0.02s)` / `FAIL |   TestFoo/SubFail (0.02s)`).
- Does **not** affect package lines (`PASS`, `ok  \tpkg\t0.012s`, `FAIL\tpkg\t0.005s`), file lines, or cover lines — verified byte-identical between true/false.
- `leaveTestPrefix: yes` is accepted as true (YAML 1.1 bool), exit 0.

## 2. `removals`

**Key finding: removals are regexp *substring deletions* applied to the fully rendered output line — after classification, labeling, Test-stripping, inner file/line styling, AND after the outer ANSI color escapes have been prepended/appended. They are not applied to raw input, and they are applied *only in colorized mode* (plain mode ignores them completely — output stays verbatim).**

Mechanics (each rule below is experimentally verified):

- Each entry is compiled with Go `regexp.MustCompile` (RE2 syntax), then applied via `ReplaceAllString(renderedLine, "")`, **sequentially in list order**:
  - `removals: [Foo, oo]` on rendered `PASS | Foo (0.00s)` → `PASS |  (0.00s)`; `[oo, Foo]` → `PASS | F (0.00s)`.
- Matching is unanchored substring. Because the target string starts with `ESC[` and ends with `ESC[0m`:
  - `^FAIL`, `^PASS`, `^START`, `^ ` **never match** (nothing is at position 0 except ESC).
  - `$` effectively never matches mid-ANSI (`0\.00s$` no-op; `^FAIL.*$` no-op).
  - Removals can corrupt the escapes: `32m` turned `ESC[32mPASS | Foo...` into `ESC[PASS | Foo...` (literal output bytes: `^[[PASS | Foo (0.00s)^[[0m`). This proves application after ANSI insertion.
- Examples (color mode, default config, removal `PASS`):
  - `--- PASS: TestFoo (0.00s)` → `ESC[32m | Foo (0.00s)ESC[0m` (label hit; note this also proves application *after* Test-stripping — content was already `Foo`).
  - `ok  \texample.com/pkg\t0.012s` → `ESC[32m | example.com/pkg ESC[0m` (the `PASS` label of the package line was hit even though the raw line contains no "PASS" — proves application after label rendering).
  - `another line with PASS inside` → `another line with  inside`.
- **Line dropping**: if the post-removal string is exactly empty, the line is omitted entirely (no newline). `removals: [".*"]` → total output is **zero bytes**. If anything remains — even only escapes — it is printed: removing `FAIL \| Bar \(0\.00s\)` leaves `ESC[31mESC[1mESC[0m\n`. (Corollary: blank input lines are also dropped in color mode; in plain mode they pass through.)
- Multiple regexps: all apply (e.g. `[START, FAIL]` blanks both labels: `ESC[90m| FooESC[0m`, `ESC[31mESC[1m | Bar (0.00s)ESC[0m`).
- Applies to every rendered line category: file lines (`foo_test` removed inside the cyan segment: `ESC[36m.goESC[0m`) and cover lines (`45` → `COVER| .0% [####______]`).
- Interaction with `leaveTestPrefix`: removals see the post-transform text. With `leaveTestPrefix: true` + removal `TestF`: `TestFoo/TestSub` → `oo/TestSub`; with default false, removal `TestF` finds nothing (`Foo/TestSub` unchanged).
- Interaction with `hide`: bare `PASS` package line vanishes under default config (`passPackageStyle.hide: true`) independently of removals.

## 3. Errors & exit codes

- **Invalid regexp** (valid YAML, e.g. `removals: ["["]`): Go panic on **stderr**, exit code **2**:
  ```
  panic: regexp: Compile(`[`): error parsing regexp: missing closing ]: `[`
  goroutine 1 [running]:
  regexp.MustCompile({0x61baf8, 0x1})  /usr/local/go/src/regexp/regexp.go:319
  github.com/kyoh86/richgo/editor/test.New()  /workspace/editor/test/test.go:19
  main.formatWriteCloser(...)  /workspace/main.go:86
  main.main()  /workspace/main.go:60
  ```
  (Stack trace reveals internal structure: `editor/test.New()` compiles removals at test.go:19.)
- **YAML syntax/escape error** (e.g. double-quoted `"FAIL \| Bar"` or `"\x1b..."`): logged to **stderr** with `log` timestamp prefix, exit code **0**, processing continues with **default config**:
  `2026/08/08 11:24:55 error unmarshaling yaml from /tmp/.../.richstyle :  yaml: line 2: found unknown escape character` (note the literal ` :  ` — space colon two spaces).
- **YAML escaping rules for regexps**: unquoted (`- 0\.00s`) and single-quoted (`- '0\.00s$'`) preserve backslashes — both work. Double-quoted scalars reject `\d`, `\|`, `\x1b`, etc. ("found unknown escape character"). Numeric entries (`- 123`) are silently coerced to the string `"123"` and work (removal `123` turned `TestFoo123` → `Foo`).

## 4. Side observations (adjacent domains, noted for the implementer)

- Plain mode appends one extra `\n` at EOF (empty input → single `\n`); color mode does not (empty input → zero bytes).
- Rendered label format: word padded to width 5 + `| ` — `START| `, `PASS | `, `FAIL | `, `SKIP | `, `COVER| `, unknown `     | `.
- "Unknown" lines inherit the previously used category's color (lightBlack after START, green after PASS, etc.) — observed but not fully characterized; left to the styling-domain agent.
